units.translation: Athene shows a quick understanding of the matter and a high sense of justice. The reading in M: ⟦1⟧ can only be explained with some difficulty: "and indeed not because he feared the wrath of some other compulsion?" The very frequent ⟦2⟧ in Aeschylus is only ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ not referred to a person. The other manuscripts, however, have ⟦5⟧, which seems more correct; accordingly Dindorf ⟦6⟧ good and clear. The scholiast, however, with ⟦7⟧ offers something else: ⟦8⟧, ⟦9⟧; (⟦10⟧ as ⟦11⟧. 774. ⟦12⟧. ⟦13⟧ ⟦14⟧⟦15⟧, ⟦16⟧. ⟦17⟧). The chorus replies that for this deed there can be no compulsion at all; cf. Aristot. Eth. N. III, 1 p. 1110, a 26: ⟦18⟧, ⟦19⟧· ⟦20⟧. On ⟦21⟧ cf. 136. 157 and especially below 466. On ⟦22⟧ (Elmsley) see on 201. — Athene is not satisfied with this, but wants first to hear the other, according to the old saying (⟦23⟧ Cic. ad Att. VII, 18; probably from the ⟦24⟧, see the exact collection of passages for the saying in Bergk Lyr. Gr. Pseudophocyl. 87): ⟦25⟧, ⟦26⟧ (⟦27⟧ added Ar. ⟦28⟧. 725) ⟦29⟧ (saying of Pittheus according to Theophrast Schol. ⟦30⟧, Bergk ibid.). "There are two persons present, so with your statement I have only half of what I must hear." Certainly correct M ⟦31⟧, against ⟦32⟧ of the other manuscripts; i.e. ⟦33⟧ instead of ⟦34⟧., Kühner-Gerth Synt. I, 279 c.
fearing the wrath of some other compulsion
he did not do this under compulsion
some things perhaps cannot be compelled
but rather one must die after suffering the most terrible things
for even the things that compelled Euripides' Alcmaeon to kill his mother appear ridiculous
you hear the speech of both
